These results demonstrate that coupling low-conjugation chromophores with local framework stabilization enables efficient cellulose RTP without extended π-conjugation, yielding a phosphorescence lifetime of 843.8 ms and a photoluminescence quantum yield of 12.8% and thereby placing the resultant material among the better-performing cellulose-based RTP systems reported to date. The superior phosphorescence is further demonstrated in time-gated optical encoding, phosphorescent hydrogels, and transparent afterglow wood. The design presented here enables low-conjugation amino chromophores to regulate the local microenvironment, offering a promising avenue for realizing cellulose-based RTP materials with prolonged afterglow.

title: Fabrication and characterization of zein/PVA nanofibers containing ferulic acid-loaded cyclodextrin metal-organic framework for enhanced sustained release and bioavailability
abstract: Advanced delivery systems are crucial for overcoming the limitations of ferulic acid (FA), including its poor water solubility and stability. This study utilized γ-cyclodextrin metal-organic framework (γ-CD-MOF) to encapsulate FA, yielding FA-loaded γ-CD-MOF (FA@CD-MOF) nanocarriers, which were subsequently incorporated into zein/polyvinyl alcohol electrospun nanofibers to construct a dual-encapsulation system. Results showed that FA@CD-MOF exhibited an average particle size of 228.36 nm, and demonstrated efficient FA encapsulation with a loading capacity of 27.39% and encapsulation efficiency of 51.76%. The composite nanofibers exhibited enhanced thermal stability and moderate anti-swelling properties. In vitro release studies demonstrated that the γ-CD-MOF effectively suppressed initial burst release of FA, and led to a sustained release profile that conformed to the Fickian diffusion mechanism. Furthermore, the composite nanofibers exhibited long-lasting antioxidant activity owing to the protective effect (nano-in-nano) of the delivery system. Notably, in vitro digestion experiments showed that the bioavailability of FA in the nanofibers reached 74.66%, a 2.9-fold increase compared to free FA (26.11%). Cytotoxicity tests on Caco-2 cells supported the remarkable biocompatibility and biosafety of the developed delivery system. Collectively, this study presents a highly promising strategy utilizing γ-CD-MOF for the controlled delivery of FA, which significantly enhances its stability and bioavailability.

title: Editorial Board
Plant GH9 enzymes and their β-1,4–glycan substrates: From in vitro EGase activity to in vivo functions
abstract: Cellulases are an increasingly important class of industrial enzymes owing to their use in a wide range of applications and sustainable products. In addition to bacteria and fungi, plants also evolved a variety of cellulases. Plant endo-β-1,4-glucanases (EGases) belong to glycoside hydrolase family 9 (GH9) enzymes, which catalyze the cleavage of internal 1,4-glycosidic bonds in plant cell wall polysaccharides. Plant EGases are divided into three types (GH9A, GH9B, GH9C), which have been implicated in cellulose biosynthesis as well as polysaccharide catabolism to remodel and disassemble cell walls in association with many developmental processes. The recent discoveries of plant GH9 family members facilitating the establishment of cellular interfaces between species encourages to explore plant EGases and their activity properties in more detail. This comprehensive review summarizes the current knowledge of plant EGases concerning their sources, activity properties, substrate specificity and suitable assays to evaluate them, as well as their native roles in plants that provide implications for their potential use in agricultural and industrial applications. The existing knowledge of the functional principles of GH9 activity is compiled and current gaps in knowledge are identified and lastly the potential in using plant EGases in the molecular breeding of GH enzymes is discussed.

title: Maltodextrin-shielded pumpkin seed protein nanoparticles formed by Maillard-induced protein modification for oral pterostilbene delivery
abstract: Plant protein nanoparticles represent promising oral carriers for hydrophobic bioactives in functional foods, yet their poor dispersibility and gastrointestinal instability limit delivery efficacy. In this study, maltodextrin (MD) was covalently conjugated with pumpkin seed protein (PP) through wet-heating glycation to construct a core-shell nanocarrier for oral pterostilbene (PTE) delivery, designated as PTE@P-M. The glycated MD-derived shell markedly improved PP solubility, reduced turbidity, and moderated surface hydrophobicity, indicating substantial remodeling of PP physicochemical properties. PTE@P-M exhibited an encapsulation efficiency of 94.47 ± 3.96% and a particle size of 249.3 ± 18.0 nm. Relative to PTE-loaded heat-treated PP (PTE@H-P), PTE@P-M retained more PTE under thermal, acidic, and Ca 2+ stress conditions and demonstrated improved in vitro digestion behavior and release kinetics. Interaction analysis and molecular docking indicated that non-covalent interactions collectively contributed to PTE stabilization within the glycated matrix. In vivo, PTE@P-M increased oral bioavailability by 3.1-fold relative to free PTE and by 1.3-fold relative to PTE@H-P. The enhanced biological efficacy of PTE@P-M was further validated in a dry eye disease model, as evidenced by increased tear secretion and alleviated ocular surface damage. Collectively, Maillard-induced MD conjugation generated a protein-core/carbohydrate-shell nanoarchitecture that enhanced PTE stability, gastrointestinal performance, and oral bioavailability.

title: Hydrogel electrolytes regulated by hydroxypropyl methylcellulose and hydroxyethyl cellulose for zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors
abstract: The practical application of zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors (ZIHSCs) is limited by the trade-off between interfacial stability and ion transport in aqueous electrolytes. Herein, two cellulose ethers with distinct substituent structures, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) and hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC), were introduced as regulatory components to construct composite hydrogel electrolytes, denoted PASMCE and PASECE, respectively. Their effects on water states, network morphology, ion transport, and electrochemical behavior were comparatively investigated. HPMC, containing relatively hydrophobic methoxy and amphiphilic hydroxypropyl substituents, promoted a denser network and stronger water confinement. These features were associated with a wider electrochemical stability window of 2.33 V, lower hydrogen-evolution and corrosion currents, and improved Zn interfacial stability. In contrast, HEC promoted a more open freeze-dried network morphology and higher ionic conductivity, enabling PASECE-based ZIHSCs to deliver a specific capacity of 105.3 mAh g -1 at 0.75 A g -1 and a maximum energy density of 115 Wh kg -1 at 825 W kg -1 . These findings demonstrate that cellulose ethers can serve as regulatory polymeric components for tailoring hydrogel electrolyte microenvironments and balancing ion transport with Zn interfacial stability.

title: Solubilization of quercetin by a modified citrus pectin fraction: Structural characterization, molecular interactions, and enhanced antioxidant activity
abstract: Quercetin is a bioactive flavonoid with diverse biological activities, but its poor aqueous solubility limits bioavailability and practical applications. In this study, the acid-modified citrus pectin fraction MCP-2 was used as a natural solubilizing matrix to improve the aqueous solubility of quercetin. Quercetin solubility reached a maximum at 1.0 mg/mL MCP-2, approximately 3.9-fold that in water. Methylation analysis and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy indicated that the MCP-2 backbone was mainly composed of galactopyranuronic acid (GalpA), methyl-esterified GalpA, and galactopyranosyl (Galp) residues, with minor rhamnopyranosyl (Rhap) residues and short GalpA-containing side chains attached to Rhap units. X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations provided consistent evidence for the formation of a stable MCP-2/quercetin complex through noncovalent interactions. Compared with quercetin and the MCP-2/quercetin physical mixture, the MCP-2/quercetin complex exhibited stronger antioxidant activity in chemical radical-scavenging assays and showed improved protection against H 2 O 2 -induced oxidative injury in HepG2 cells. Overall, this study elucidates the mechanism of MCP-2-mediated quercetin solubilization and provides a natural polysaccharide-based strategy for improving the aqueous solubility and functional performance of poorly water-soluble flavonoids.

title: Impact of ring-opening chemistry on the local chain mobility of arabinoxylan
abstract: Periodate oxidation and borohydride reduction has been put forward as a modification that increases the flexibility of polysaccharide chains, thereby lowering the glass transition temperature. To investigate whether the reaction is able to increase the chain mobility of a branched polysaccharide such as arabinoxylan (AX), ring-opened dialdehyde AX (DAX), and dialcohol AX (DiolAX) were studied with solid-state NMR techniques. For materials equilibrated at 53% relative humidity, it was found that DiolAX exhibits increased chain mobility, observed as a two- and three-fold decrease in the proton relaxation time in the rotating frame ( T 1 ρ H ), compared to AX and DAX. From measurements of the proton dipolar linewidth, the narrowest linewidth, thus highest mobility, was observed at the C5/ring-opened C2-C3 region of DiolAX. This is expected largely from an increase in mobility of the ring-opened C2-C3 environments. When the materials were equilibrated at < 10% RH, the dynamics became slower and more similar across AX, DAX and DiolAX.

title: Durable and self-adaptive cotton cellulose fabrics grafted with zwitterionic telomer brushes for anti-liquid and antifouling
abstract: Antiadhesive cotton cellulose fabrics have attracted increasing attention in medicine, hygiene, and daily life. However, their practical applications are often limited by the insufficient bacterial antiadhesion capacity, inadequate functionality, and poor durability. To address these challenges, a novel cotton cellulose fabric grafted with zwitterionic telomer brushes consisting of fluorinated segments, zwitterionic precursors and silane coupling agent was prepared. Such fabrics exhibit environment-responsive self-adaptive performance. When used in air, the cotton cellulose fabrics are dominated by low-surface-energy fluorine motif from dodecafluoroheptyl methacrylate (DFMA), resisting the adhesion of various kinds of liquid. While used underwater, the cotton cellulose fabrics transforms into the zwitterionic layer by the rapid hydrolysis of tertiary carboxybetaine triisopropylsilyl ester ethyl acrylate (TCBSi), exhibiting oleophobicity (oil contact angles underwater increased from 27° to 123°) and antibacterial functions to Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) (antibacterial efficiency >97%). Moreover, the silane coupling agent (3-mercaptopropyl trimethoxysilane, KH590) can form covalent bonds with cotton cellulose fabrics, significantly enhances the washing durability of the modified fabrics. This strategy contributes to the design and fabrication of anti-liquid and antifouling cotton cellulose fabrics for medicine, hygiene, and other fields.

title: Lamellar-structured anisotropic sodium alginate/montmorillonite aerogels with mechanical robustness and flame-retardant thermal insulation
abstract: Lightweight, flame-retardant, and thermally insulating bio-based materials are required for thermal protection in buildings; however, sodium alginate (SA) aerogels are mechanically fragile and prone to drying shrinkage. Herein, anisotropic SA/montmorillonite (SA/MMT) aerogels were fabricated via freeze-casting, post-freeze ionic crosslinking in a low-temperature CaCl₂/EtOH bath, and air drying. The key innovation lies in the MMT-assisted stabilization of the freeze-cast lamellar skeleton, which preserves a highly porous framework during air drying while enhancing mechanical robustness and fire resistance. Increasing the MMT/SA ratio from 0 to 80 wt% reduced radial shrinkage from 13.6% to 4.2% while maintaining porosity above 95% and increased the axial specific modulus from 65.4 to 174.5 MPa cm 3 g -1 . The LOI increased from 29 to 81.2, whereas pHRR and THR decreased from 28.8 to 13.0 W g -1 and from 2.91 to 1.41 kJ/g, respectively. The optimized SA/MMT-80 aerogel exhibited a density of 0.09 g/cm 3 and a thermal conductivity below 0.05 W/(m K). XPS and Raman analyses of the post-combustion residues revealed a stabilized carbonaceous-inorganic residual barrier, with the I D /I G ratio decreasing from 2.82 to 1.76, while TG-FTIR indicated a possible complementary gas-phase dilution effect associated with the released CO₂. These results establish a structurally stabilized air-drying route for multifunctional SA-based aerogels.

title: Starch crystal and fine structure govern the digestive behavior of V-type complexes with proteolytic peptide: Dynamic structural evolution and sustained release during digestion
abstract: This study investigated the regulatory mechanisms of different crystal and fine-structured starches on the dynamic structural evolution and peptide sustained release of the starch-wheat proteolytic peptide (WPP) V-type complex during in vitro digestion. Maize starch was predominantly short-chain (A-chain 34.66%), forming a highly ordered V-type complex with WPP (resistant starch 27.37%, d Bragg = 12.37 nm). During digestion, its terminal intestinal digested products had the highest molecular weight (4.57 × 10 3 Da), with a long-chain (DP ≥ 37) residual rate of 11.13%, and exhibited the slowest WPP release (precipitation retention rate of 71.2%). Potato starch structure was dominated by long chains (B1 chain >64%), forming a relatively loose complex structure (resistant starch 22.34%, d Bragg = 11.14 nm). Its digested products had the smallest molecular weight (3.43 × 10 3 Da), with the lowest long-chain residual rate (3.8%) and the fastest WPP release (retention rate 58.1%). Pea starch possessed structural characteristics intermediate between maize and potato starch. Its complex contained 23.42% resistant starch with d Bragg = 10.63 nm. After digestion, the molecular weight of the digested product was 3.81 × 10 3 Da, the long-chain residual rate was 12.18%, and the WPP retention rate was 62.3%. Consequently, maize starch with its rich short-chain fine structure formed the densest V-type complex, conferring superior anti-digestibility and sustained peptide release.

title: Cellulose-based dual-network hydrogels combining reversible Schiff base interactions and photopolymerized covalent networks
abstract: Polysaccharide-based hydrogels have attracted considerable interest for biomedical applications due to their inherent biocompatibility, structural flexibility, and renewable origin. Among them, cellulose and its derivatives represent particularly promising building blocks; however, the limited mechanical stability and rapid degradation of conventional polysaccharide hydrogels under physiological conditions remain major challenges for their practical implementation. In this work, we report the development of cellulose-based dual-network hydrogels combining reversible Schiff base interactions and photopolymerized covalent networks through the rational integration of selectively oxidized and methacrylated cellulose (CoxM) or hydroxypropyl cellulose (HoxM) with methacrylated gelatin (GM). The first network was formed by dynamic Schiff base interactions, while the second, permanent network was formed by riboflavin-mediated UV (365 nm) photopolymerization of methacrylate groups. In addition to its structural contribution, GM acted as a co-initiator by promoting radical generation through its primary amine groups, eliminating the need for conventional cytotoxic photoinitiators. Rheological and mechanical investigations demonstrated that hydrogel properties could be tailored the oxidation chemistry and methacrylation degree of the cellulose derivatives. The resulting dual-network hydrogels exhibited enhanced viscoelasticity and structural integrity, making them promising candidates for tissue engineering, wound healing, and controlled drug delivery, pending further biological validation.

title: Self-powered chitosan-based nanofibrous intelligent packaging for monitoring of strawberry freshness
abstract: Strawberries are susceptible to water loss, microbial spoilage, and quality deterioration during storage and transportation, resulting in a shortened shelf life. Intelligent packaging integrating active preservation and freshness indication can delay deterioration while providing quality feedback. Humidity variations caused by respiration and transpiration are closely associated with strawberry quality deterioration, yet their conversion into real-time data feedback remains challenging for conventional systems. Herein, a self-powered humidity-sensitive chitosan-based nanofibrous packaging material was fabricated via electrospinning. Deacetylated chitin nanocrystals (D-ChNCs) nanoframe reinforcement and tea polyphenols (TP) functionalization synergistically constructed a CTS/PEO/D-ChNCs/TP three-dimensional nanofibrous network. The heterogeneous interfaces and polar functional groups promoted triboelectric charge accumulation, enabling the triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) based on this membrane to achieve an open-circuit voltage approaching 180 V. Benefiting from the abundant hydrophilic functional groups and large contact area, the TENG converted packaging humidity variations into voltage signals. As the relative humidity (RH) increased from 50% to 80%, the output voltage decreased linearly (R 2 = 0.993), enabling reliable humidity sensing. The D-ChNCs/TP-functionalized membrane exhibited antioxidant and antibacterial activities, delaying strawberry deterioration for 6 days. Meanwhile, the TENG output signal was strongly correlated with weight loss, firmness, and total soluble solids, enabling self-powered classification of strawberry freshness.

title: CAZyme-guided modification of cactus and regional polysaccharides for food hydrocolloid applications
abstract: Food-hydrocolloid performance depends on polymer architecture and processing history rather than ingredient name alone. This critical narrative review evaluates CAZyme-guided modification of cactus-derived pectic materials and related regional polysaccharides for food hydrocolloid applications. Opuntia mucilage and pectic fractions are the focal substrates; non-cactus pectins provide the closest mechanistic evidence, and arabinoxylan is retained only as a bounded comparison for substitution and oxidative crosslinking. Starch is considered only as a limited process benchmark and is not used to infer cactus-polysaccharide behavior. The evidence is organized as four incomplete links: candidate selection, enzyme-to-edit, edit-to-property, and application validation. No study yet completes this chain for a food hydrocolloid, and cactus-associated microbiomes have not been shown to be superior CAZyme reservoirs. Candidate selection therefore requires reaction-specific annotation, multidomain and genomic-context analysis where relevant, expression, real-substrate kinetics, edit-state measurement, side-activity testing, and comparison with conventional hydrocolloids. Metagenomic discovery is treated as one prospective route to new catalysts, not as the evidentiary foundation of the current enzyme-to-material literature or as a validated production platform.

title: Self-healing and reprocessable cellulose-based bioplastics based on side-group engineering approach
abstract: Developing cellulose-based bioplastics that combine mechanical robustness, self-healing, and reprocessability remains challenging because the dense hydrogen-bonded structure of cellulose provides cohesion but restricts the chain mobility required for interfacial reconstruction. Here, we report a side-group engineering strategy that balances these competing requirements by integrating flexible long aliphatic chains, metal-responsive aromatic groups, and Zn 2+ -mediated reversible interactions within a single cellulose-derived network. To implement this strategy, indole-3-acetic acid and oleic acid were sequentially grafted onto cellulose, followed by the introduction of Zn 2+ to construct reversible dynamic junctions. The long aliphatic chains disrupted ordered chain packing and promoted molecular rearrangement, whereas the indole-derived aromatic groups enabled reversible network reconstruction. At an aromatic-group-to-Zn 2+ molar ratio of 10:1, the resulting bioplastic achieved a tensile strength of 18.31 MPa and a tensile-strength healing efficiency of 92.14% after DMAc-assisted interfacial wetting followed by thermal treatment at 80 °C for 2 h. After four reprocessing cycles, it retained a tensile strength of 18.27 MPa and a tensile-strength healing efficiency of 90.53%. These results demonstrate that synergistically regulating chain mobility and reversible cohesion is an effective molecular design strategy for constructing mechanically robust, self-healing, and reprocessable cellulose-based bioplastics.

title: Supramolecular α-cyclodextrin-mediated fully bio-based Pickering emulsions as plant-derived biopesticide erucamide delivery systems enabling sustainable crop protection
abstract: The novel plant-derived biopesticide erucamide (Eru) holds promise for controlling plant bacterial diseases, yet its poor water solubility and formulation instability limit practical application. Here, supramolecular aggregate particles in aqueous solution via host-guest recognition between α-cyclodextrin (α-CD) and Eru were constructed. These particles serve as the sole stabilizer to emulsify a carvacrol (Car) oil phase pre-loaded with additional Eru, yielding a surfactant-free, all-natural Pickering emulsion (PE). Compared with a conventional suspension concentrate (SC), the PE exhibits superior wettability and adhesion on superhydrophobic rice leaves, improving pesticide utilization efficiency. In addition, the PE exhibited potent inhibitory activity against the mycelial growth of nine fungal pathogens, with EC 50 values ranging from 8.2 to 37.2 μg/mL. This antifungal activity is closely associated with the incorporated Car, as the SC formulation without Car showed no inhibition against these strains under the same conditions. Moreover, in a 14-day greenhouse trial on rice seedlings, the PE treatment resulted in a 17.2% increase in root length, 5.6% increase in shoot length, and 17.8% increase in aboveground fresh weight relative to the untreated control. This study provides a distinctive paradigm for developing eco-friendly multifunctional agrochemical formulations, particularly for hydrophobic, long-alkyl-chain active ingredients, to overcome solubility and utilization challenges.

title: Thermoresponsive shrinkage-driven chitosan hydrogel boosts sustainable Cu2+ removal
abstract: Developing adsorbents with efficient regeneration and long-term stability and reusability remains a critical challenge for sustainable heavy-metal removal. In this study, chitosan (CS) was molecularly engineered into a thermoresponsive hydrogel (TR-ICS g ) capable of integrating efficient Cu 2+ adsorption with rapid, low-consumption regeneration. Under thermal stimulation, enhanced interactions among hydrophobic alkyl groups promoted hydrogel dehydration, resulting in pronounced volume shrinkage. Further, during regeneration, this thermally induced shrinkage enabled efficient elution with only 200 mL·g -1 of 0.1 M HCl, reducing acid consumption by 67.2% compared to the swollen state. The shrunken TR-ICS g achieved a Cu 2+ desorption efficiency of 92.7% within 5 min, demonstrating rapid regeneration under low-eluent conditions. Under a standardized adsorption-desorption protocol (pH 6.0, 25 °C, initial Cu 2+ concentration of 200 mg·L -1 , 10 min), TR-ICS g sustained 20 consecutive cycles within 300 min, achieving a cumulative Cu 2+ uptake of 905 mg·g -1 , while the single-cycle uptake decreased only modestly from 52.4 to 38.2 mg·g -1 . This study provides a scalable, low-consumption regeneration strategy for sustainable and continuous heavy-metal wastewater treatment.

title: Corrigendum to “A promising hierarchical-pore cellulose scaffold for cell culture inspired by wood's multiscale architecture” [Carbohydrate Polymers 373, 124656 (2026)]
Biofermentation-induced cellulose integration for sustainable basalt-based organic-inorganic smart protective textiles
abstract: Sustainable wearable protective textiles integrating mechanical protection, monitoring, and visual feedback are desirable for healthcare and personal protection. However, multifunctional integration remains challenging because rigid inorganic fibers are difficult to integrate with conductive polypyrrole (PPy) and cellulose-based layers. Inspired by climbing plants, a biofermentation-induced cellulose integration strategy was developed to construct a basalt textile. Polypyrrole-coated basalt fabric was biofermented with bacterial cellulose (BC) to form a basalt/PPy/BC composite (BPB), the primary platform for mechanical protection and piezoresistive sensing. A self-assembled cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) layer was deposited on BPB to obtain basalt/PPy/BC/CNC (BPBC), adding structural-color feedback while retaining electrical responses. BPB exhibits an air permeability of 472.3 mm·s -1 , high mechanical robustness (maximum tensile force of 1390.6 N, 438.2 N bursting force, 24.4 N puncture force), good impact resistance (71.64% attenuation after 50 consecutive impacts), and piezoresistive sensing (-0.0448 and -0.0222 kPa -1 ). With the assistance of a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN), the platform enabled real-time hazard warning (98.3% within-dataset accuracy). This work provides a cellulose-mediated strategy for multifunctional cellulose-based smart protective textiles.

title: Improving the processability and digestion resistance of rice starch gel through linear chain-ferulic acid V-type complexation and branch-mediated crosslinking
abstract: Ferulic acid (FA) reduces starch digestibility but disrupts gel network, limiting its application in gel strength-reliant products. Rice starch was sequentially modified by pullulanase and transglucosidase to generate linear chains with a few branches (LCFBs), which were complexed with 0-2.0% FA to clarify how intermolecular interactions regulated the trade-off between gel strength and digestion resistance. At 0.5% FA, the hardness of modified starch gel remained at 98.2 g, whereas that of native starch gel decreased from 122.0 to 76.1 g. Moreover, the latter could not be shaped into blocks at 1.0% FA. Concurrently, compared with estimated glycemic index (76.6) of native starch gel, modified starch-0.5%FA complexation achieved an 11.10% reduction, while native starch-0.5%FA showed only a 5.61% decrease. The main chains of LCFBs favored V-type complexation with FA, while their branches promoted intermolecular crosslinking to preserve network integrity. This mode increased single helix from 5.92% to 9.40%, and relative crystallinity from 10.47% to 11.73%. In contrast, native starch-0.5%FA gel, despite exhibiting some V-type complex formation, suffered significant loss of ordered structures, which constituted the primary cause of reduced gel strength. Therefore, V-type complexation between LCFBs and 0.5% FA, coupled with branch-mediated crosslinking, effectively preserved gel strength and enhanced digestion resistance.

title: Swelling-programmed hemicellulose/chitosan cryogels with tunable porous transport for rapid selective adsorption
abstract: The sustainable porous materials are highly desirable for achieving rapid and selective ionic separation in water purification, yet the relationship between swelling-induced pore evolution and transport behavior remains insufficiently understood. Here, a swelling-mediated porous transport strategy is reported for biomass-derived cryogels. By regulating the swelling state of hydrogel precursors before freeze-drying, dialdehyde hemicellulose/chitosan cryogels (DHC) with programmable interconnected pores were constructed. The optimized cryogels showed ultrafast water uptake (<1 s), reversible compressibility under 80% strain, and stable porous transport during repeated operation. Swelling-programmed pore architectures accelerated dye diffusion and adsorption kinetics, enabling DHC-240 to reach a maximum Orange G (OG) adsorption capacity of 785.64 mg/g and rapid separation within 1 min. In mixed dye systems, DHC-240 showed high ionic selectivity, with selectivity coefficients up to 3319. Molecular simulation revealed charge-dependent adsorption. Anionic OG and fluorescein sodium (FS) maintained stable binding distances of 5.64 and 7.13 Å, whereas cationic dyes showed unstable, energetically unfavorable interactions. Energy decomposition highlighted docking interaction energy as the dominant contribution (-33.8 kcal/mol), and free-energy analysis confirmed favorable OG binding (-2.1 kcal/mol) versus unfavorable methylene blue binding (+1.6 kcal/mol). This work establishes swelling-regulated pore programming for transport-controlled molecular separation.

title: A V-type starch-lycopene complex with enhanced cis-lycopene content alleviates hyperglycemia and glycogen fragility in type 2 diabetic db/db mice via gut microbiota
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a major global health challenge. Resistant starch type 5 (RS5), formed by complexing starch with guest components into V-type crystalline structures, represents a promising approach for glycemia control. Native lycopene has anti-diabetic potential but limited bioactivity. Here we developed a V-type corn starch-lycopene RS5 complex (CS-LYC) and evaluated its effects in T2DM db/db mice, focusing on glycemic control and gut microbiota-liver glycogen connection. CS-LYC contained 26.07% resistant starch and 11.8 mg/g lycopene, with complexation promoting isomerization to the more bioactive (13Z)-isomer and increasing lycopene accumulation in both plasma and liver in vivo. In db/db mice, CS-LYC improved insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis by remodeling gut microbiota (enriching Akkermansia and Alistipes) and increasing metabolites (short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives), subsequently maintaining intestinal barrier function and stimulating GLP-1 secretion. Through the gut-liver axis, this GLP-1 activated the hepatic PI3K/AKT pathway and increased the proportion of stable glycogen α particles, thereby reducing glycogen fragility, with fecal microbiota transplantation further confirming that these effects were mediated by gut microbiota. Collectively, CS-LYC alleviates T2DM via the gut-liver GLP-1/PI3K-AKT axis, offering a new dietary strategy for diabetes management.

title: Isolation of elementary nanofibrils of cellulose from non-structural plant cells via hydrothermal processing
abstract: Abstract The isolation of cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs), a promising precursor for sustainable and high-performance materials, has relied on chemically intensive, energy-demanding processes. As these processes were originally designed for the isolation of CNFs from wood, we herein show that the intrinsic ultrastructure of non-structural plant cells provides unique opportunities, namely direct access to loosely organized cellulose nanonetworks. We demonstrate that this loose nanofibrillar tissue can be transformed into CNFs with sizes down to elementary nanofibrils (∼4 nm) at high yields (reaching ∼32%) under exceptionally mild hydrothermal conditions. Three distinct plants were evaluated and the physicochemical properties of the obtained nanonetworks and corresponding CNFs were thoroughly studied, including the hydrodynamics of the resulting gels. Films prepared from the obtained CNFs showed similar performance to those obtained from conventionally isolated wood-based CNFs. Overall, this study demonstrates that CNFs can be obtained through low-intensity, hazard-free, processes from widely available biomass. Thus, this approach offers a unique shift in the range of opportunities to produce CNFs facilitating the integration of their use into the food supply chain, biomedical applications, and other regulatory-constrained applications.

title: Reframing starch innovation for food security, sustainability, and metabolic health: From crop design to precision nutrition
abstract: Starch remains the caloric backbone of global diets, yet its long-term security is challenged by climate instability, dependence on a few staple crops, unsustainable processing practices, and the growing burden of diet-related metabolic diseases. Although major advances have been made in starch genetics, crop management, processing, and nutritional design, these developments are often discussed in isolation. This review adopts an integrated food-system perspective that follows starch from production to consumption and emphasizes how decisions across the value chain jointly shape functionality, resource efficiency, and metabolic outcomes. We synthesize progress in four interconnected areas: (i) genetic and agronomic strategies to improve starch yield, quality, and stress tolerance; (ii) diversification, preservation, and circular valorization of starch resources; (iii) structural and processing approaches for resistant starch and glycemic control; and (iv) emerging technologies including synthetic biology, artificial intelligence (AI), plant-microbiome engineering, and starch-based intelligent materials. We also identify key translational bottlenecks, including limited structure-to-function prediction, scale-up constraints, and regulatory and equity issues surrounding next-generation starch technologies. By integrating plant biotechnology, food engineering and nutritional physiology, this review provides a framework for developing resilient, sustainable, and health-oriented food systems.

title: Octenyl succinic anhydride starch-lemon essential oil coatings with superior preservative effects on fresh foods
abstract: Starch-based coatings that incorporate active agents have potential to prolong the shelf-life of fresh foods. In this study, coatings made from maize or pea starches modified by octenyl succinic anhydride (OSA) esterification and incorporating lemon essential oil (LEO) are shown to have better preservative effects for fresh foods than coatings made from the unmodified starches. OSA esterification enhanced the stability of dispersion of LEO in starch emulsions, thereby facilitating the formation of starch-LEO films with better morphology. Starch-LEO inclusion complexes were formed in the preparation of starch-LEO films, especially in those made with OSA-pea starch. Films made from OSA-starch-LEO emulsions had better functional properties than the corresponding films made from the respective unmodified starch. Accordingly, the OSA-pea starch-LEO coatings showed the best preservative effects on the quality and shelf-life of fresh apricots and pork. This study demonstrated that OSA modification of starch shows promise as a way for preparing starch-based coatings incorporating essential oils and having good preservative effects.

title: Heat moisture treatment modifies amaranth, quinoa, and taro starches via reorganizing granular architecture and driving aggregation
abstract: Amaranth, quinoa, and taro starches have very small granule sizes, which are desirable in certain applications. Heat-moisture treatment (HMT) could modify their properties by changing the granular architecture but maintain the technical advantages related to small granule size. The study intended to investigate how starch structure modulated the diverse HMT modifications. The results suggested that, beyond the granular size, both amylose and amylopectin played important roles in the HMT modification of starch. Upon HMT, amylose might strengthen the packing of starch granules via interacting with amylopectin. Unit chains with chain lengths of 13-24 glucose residues and fingerprint B-chains in amylopectin were negatively related to the reduction of ordered structures upon HMT. Using a method newly developed based on the building block-backbone model, the HMT-induced alteration in the conformation of the branched backbone of amylopectin was characterized. For maize and taro starches, the HMT had relatively conservative effects on the branch distribution in starch granules. The branch distribution in the granule of potato starch was altered upon the transformation of its polymorphism. HMT resulted in severe aggregation of small-granule starches, which exerted a superimposed effect on the modification of starch properties.

title: Corrigendum to “A one-step approach to make cellulose-based hydrogels of various transparency and swelling degrees” [Carbohydrate Polymers, Volume 186, 15 April 2018, Pages 208-216]
Corrigendum to “Chitosan-assisted MOFs dispersion via covalent bonding interaction toward highly efficient removal of heavy metal ions from wastewaters” [Carbohydrate Polymers, 277 (2022), 118809]
Maltooligosaccharide-forming amylases improve steamed bread quality and anti-staling effects via coordinated fermentation enhancement and starch structural remodeling
abstract: Steamed bread quality deterioration during storage, especially texture hardening caused by starch structural changes, remains a major challenge in wheat-based fermented foods. This study investigated the effects of maltooligosaccharide-forming amylases (MFAs) with different product specificities on steamed bread quality, fermentation behavior, and starch structural properties. Results showed that all MFAs significantly improved product quality, increasing specific volume by 10.92-15.28% and reducing hardness by 18.68-26.04%, with maltopentaose- (MFAbs-G5) and maltohexaose-forming amylases (MFAbs-G6) exhibiting superior performance. MFAs treatment enhanced starch hydrolysis, increasing fermentable sugars (G1-G3) and maltooligosaccharides (G4-G6), which was associated with improved gas production, retention capacity, and dough expansion. Meanwhile, MFAs reduced molecular weight, altered starch chain-length distribution toward shorter glucan chains, and decreased relative crystallinity. During refrigerated storage, MFA-treated samples exhibited attenuated texture deterioration. After 7 days of storage, the hardness values of the MFAbs-G5 and MFAbs-G6 groups were 71.16% and 73.30% of the control, respectively. Overall, MFAs improved steamed bread quality and storage stability through coordinated regulation of fermentation performance and starch structural characteristics. These findings provide insights into the potential application of product-specific MFAs as enzyme-based improvers for wheat-based fermented foods.

title: In situ construction of bacterial cellulose-based hydrogels: Mechanisms, functionalization strategies, and biomedical applications
abstract: The past several decades have witnessed great success in bacterial cellulose (BC) and its hydrogel composites in terms of both broad and in-depth basic research and potential biomedical applications. Inspired by the natural properties of microorganisms, in situ biosynthesis strategies are receiving increasing attention for the structural and functional design of BC-based hydrogels. This review discusses these strategies with emphasis on their fabrication processes and underlying mechanisms. Structure-property relationships governing BC-based hydrogels-molecular structure, nanofibrous architecture, biocompatibility, mechanical performance, and hydration behavior are examined to establish a process-structure-property framework. Biomedical applications including wound healing, drug delivery, osteogenic therapy, bioelectronic sensing, and cardiovascular repair are critically evaluated with quantitative comparison to conventional materials. Finally, challenges and future prospects in standardized characterization, scalable manufacturing, biosafety assessment, and clinical translation are discussed. This review provides a mechanism-oriented guide for developing BC-based hydrogels via in situ strategies for next-generation healthcare applications.

title: Electric field technologies for polysaccharide extraction and structural modification: Electrode- and induction-mediated energy-delivery systems
abstract: Electric field technologies are increasingly used to extract and modify polysaccharides, yet comparisons remain difficult because systems differ in energy delivery, operating conditions, and mechanistic evidence. This review classifies pulsed electric fields, moderate electric fields, and ohmic heating as electrode-mediated technologies, and induced electric fields as induction-mediated technologies. It compares their effects across starch, pectin, chitosan, plant gums, dietary fibers, marine polysaccharides, and related matrices from molecular to network scales. Reported responses include depolymerization, changes in crystallinity and short-range order, particle restructuring, and network reorganization, with consequences for extraction yield, digestibility, rheology, thermal behavior, and emulsification. These outcomes arise from coupled thermal, electrochemical, polarization-related, and transport phenomena whose relative contributions depend on field parameters, conductivity, temperature history, pH, reactor configuration, and substrate structure. Direct mechanistic support is strongest for heating, current flow, and selected electrode-interface effects, whereas polarization, ion transport, and direct field-induced bond cleavage remain incompletely verified. An evidence-weighted energy-structure-function framework is proposed to guide condition-aware comparisons. Standardized reporting, matched controls, multiscale characterization, and scale-up assessment are needed to enable predictive process design and industrial translation.

title: Advanced chitosan multifunctional sustainable platforms for targeted therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): Progress and future directions
Ferric ion-mediated sodium carboxymethyl cellulose/metal-phenolic dual-network nanogels for probiotic encapsulation and delivery
Sequential electrospun trilayer fibrous pullulan membranes for a combined anti-virulence and microbiota-supportive therapy of bacterial vaginosis
Chitosan-based hydrogels for chronic wound healing: From multifunctional modification to microenvironment regulation and clinical translation
abstract: The management of chronic wounds remains a critical challenge in biomedical research owing to their complex pathophysiology and unmet clinical needs. As a naturally derived cationic polysaccharide, chitosan exhibits exceptional biocompatibility, biodegradability, antimicrobial efficacy, and tissue-repair capabilities, making it an ideal building block for advanced wound care. When crosslinked into a three-dimensional hydrogel network that retains water effectively and mimics the extracellular matrix, this biomaterial provides an ideal platform for chronic wound management. Consequently, recent research has increasingly focused on functional chitosan-based hydrogel systems, with strategies such as chemical modification and stimuli-responsive design intensively explored to precisely regulate the wound microenvironment and accelerate tissue regeneration. This review is organized around three core objectives: (i) multifunctional modification, (ii) microenvironment regulation, and (iii) clinical translation. It systematically summarizes the pathophysiological characteristics of chronic wounds, outlines methods for preparing chitosan-based hydrogels, and comprehensively discusses their applications in chronic wound repair. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging functionalization strategies, such as incorporating TCM active ingredients, loading nanozymes and single-atom enzymes, and designing multi-stimuli-responsive systems. It provides a critical discussion of clinical translation, highlighting current challenges and realistic future perspectives to guide the rational design and development of high-performance chitosan-based hydrogels for chronic wound therapy.

title: Natural polysaccharides in pancreatic cancer therapy: From immunomodulation and gut microbiota regulation to metabolic intervention
abstract: Natural polysaccharides derived from plants, fungi, macroalgae, cyanobacteria, and other marine microorganisms have attracted increasing interest as adjuvant candidates for pancreatic cancer management due to their biocompatibility, structural diversity, and multi-target activities. This review consolidates current knowledge on their anti-pancreatic cancer activities, integrating findings from in vitro, in vivo, and mechanistic studies. We delineate the multi-level regulatory networks through which polysaccharides exert anti-tumor effects via four interconnected mechanisms: direct actions on cancer cells including proliferation inhibition, apoptosis and ferroptosis induction, cell cycle arrest, metastasis suppression, and autophagy modulation; immunomodulation via M1 macrophage polarization, natural killer cell activation, and cytotoxic T lymphocyte mediated killing; restoration of gut microbial homeostasis through beneficial taxa enrichment, intestinal barrier integrity enhancement, short-chain fatty acid elevation, and lipopolysaccharide driven inflammation reduction; and indirect tumor suppression by ameliorating obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus. The polysaccharide gut microbiota axis emerges as a critical hub integrating these pathways. Structure-activity relationship analysis indicates that low molecular weight, high galacturonic acid content, arabinose and galactose richness, and sulfation may influence activity, although robust attribution requires structurally defined polysaccharides. More than twenty well characterized polysaccharides are documented, with several showing synergistic effects with chemotherapeutics. Despite encouraging preclinical evidence, challenges remain in structural characterization, bioavailability, and clinical validation.

title: Starch nanocrystals as programmable interfacial building blocks for pickering emulsion gels: Assembly mechanisms, hierarchical structures, and food applications
Structural characteristics and α-amylase and α-glucosidase inhibition of arabinoxylans released from fresh corn bran
From single chains to bulk materials: Unraveling polysaccharide hierarchies with atomic force microscopy
Heterologous production of structurally distinct levans in an optimized Paenibacillus polymyxa chassis
abstract: Levan is a bacterial β-fructan exopolysaccharide that is highly valued for its applications as a prebiotic, natural sweetener, and adhesive. Levan is synthesized by levansucrases (EC 2.4.1.10), which utilize the energy from sucrose hydrolysis to polymerize fructose. To establish an efficient microbial platform for levan production, we employed the non-pathogenic soil bacterium, Paenibacillus polymyxa, a natural producer of the exopolysaccharides paenan and levan. By sequential deletion of genes involved in paenan biosynthesis, extracellular proteolysis, levan degradation, and foam formation, we created a production chassis with enhanced levan production. In batch fermentation, the optimized strain produced 30.2 g⋅L⁻¹ of ultrapure levan (yield: 0.30 g⋅g⁻¹), which was further increased by 82 % using a fed-batch strategy. To expand the structural diversity of levans, levansucrases from various bacterial strains were integrated into the genome of P. polymyxa. Seven of the eight variants successfully produced high-purity levan at titers from 1.8 to 26.3 g⋅L⁻¹. The obtained levans were structurally diverse, with molecular weights from 5.5 to 30.9 MDa and branching degrees of 9 to 16 %. This engineered P. polymyxa chassis enables the production of structurally tailored levans under standardized conditions and provides a versatile platform for recombinant exopolysaccharide biosynthesis.

title: Structural characterization of an Alhagi honey polysaccharide and its activity against alcoholic fatty liver disease through the AMPK/PI3K–Akt/NF-κB signaling pathway
Structure-informed immunomodulation: how polysaccharides modulate selected components of the tumour immune microenvironment
From bacteria to photopolymer: Maleimide-functionalized dextrans for initiator-free and donor-acceptor photopolymerization

Tween 80 reorganizes the chitosan precursor microenvironment to enhance genipin crosslinking and hydrogel performance
abstract: Chitosan–genipin hydrogels are attractive for biomedical applications, yet their network formation is limited by the poor aqueous dispersion of genipin and the aggregated colloidal state of the chitosan precursor. Addition of surfactants often helps by solubilising the hydrophobic crosslinker. This study combines two factors: addition of a non-ionic surfactant (Tween 80) and use of a higher-ionic-strength acetate buffer. Results showed that Tween 80 acts predominantly by reorganising the chitosan precursor microenvironment, through an effect decoupled from bulk viscosity. Dynamic light scattering showed that Tween 80 redistributed micron-scale chitosan aggregates into nanoscale assemblies (~40–85 nm), while acetate buffering compacted the chitosan chains via ionic-strength screening. The phase into which Tween 80 was added was critical. With the total amount fixed, adding Tween 80 to the chitosan phase raised the crosslinking rate by 6.2-fold, whereas adding it to the genipin phase gave little benefit, likely because genipin became constrained inside Tween 80 micelles. The reorganised precursor reached the gel point up to 45.5% sooner. Acting together, buffering and Tween 80 produced a more PBS-stable network with up to 2.8-fold higher compressive strength. These findings identify precursor-state control as the governing mechanism and provide a transferable strategy for tuning chitosan-based hydrogels.

Influence of the helical cavity diameter on the loading capacity and sustained release potential of V-amylose–α-linolenic acid complexes
abstract: V-amylose, a single-helical form of amylose, provides an enzyme-responsive platform for encapsulating bioactive compounds. However, the influence of its helical cavity diameter on α-linolenic acid (ALA) delivery potential remains poorly understood. This study investigated how cavity diameter affects the loading capacity and sustained release potential of V-amylose–ALA complexes. V6-, V7-, and V8-amylose were prepared by guest-induced crystallization and loaded with ALA in acetone. XRD, FTIR, and solid-state NMR confirmed the preservation of the single-helical structure after complexation and the formation of V-amylose–ALA inclusion helices. V7–ALA complexes showed the greatest ALA loading capacity (26 mg/g) and enhanced thermal stability. In vitro digestion suggested that the V7–ALA complexes contained the highest proportion of slowly digestible starch (45.2%), indicating superior sustained release potential. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that the enhanced loading performance of V7–ALA complexes may arise from a balance among host–guest interaction strength (−663 kJ/mol), binding-induced cavity distortion, and solvation effects. These findings provide mechanistic insights into the cavity-dependent performance of V-amylose–ALA complexes and support the rational design of V-amylose–based delivery systems.

Access to low-molar-mass celluloses from cotton linters through combined electron-beam irradiation / β-elimination treatments
abstract: Celluloses with very low molar mass and well-defined molar mass distributions represent an underexplored fraction of the polymer. Controlled degradation of cellulose into low-molar-mass segments are still a challenge due to its recalcitrant structure. A combined oxidation/β-elimination strategy provides an efficient way to generate such low-molar-mass celluloses. In this study, electron beam irradiation (EBI) was investigated as depolymerization strategy for cotton linters, followed by alkaline β-elimination to promote further carbonyl-induced chain cleavage. To assess whether irradiation-induced degradation could be chemically enhanced, cellulose was treated with H2O2, FeSO4/H2O2, KI and CuSO4, prior to irradiation at varying doses. Depolymerization and carbonyl-group formation were monitored by molar-mass-resolved fluorescence labeling and multidetector gel permeation chromatography. Notably, irradiation alone effectively reduced the molar mass, yielding results comparable to those obtained for pretreated samples, which had little or no effect. Additionally, a repeated EBI/β-elimination sequence produced low-molar-mass cellulose with the lowest DP (~61) and the highest proportion of chains with DP below 100 while maintaining low dispersity. In summary, EBI followed by β-elimination, including repeated cycles, offers an interesting route to generate low-DP cellulose fragments with good uniformity, presenting potential for value-added applications.

title: Structure-dependent periodate oxidation of schizophyllan templates the growth of “head-and-tail” gold and palladium nanoparticles
abstract: Polysaccharides are attractive green reagents for the synthesis of metal nanoparticles, but typically yield isotropic, polyhedral particles. Here, we show that periodate-oxidized schizophyllan, a (1 → 3)-β-D-glucan bearing (1 → 6)-β- d -glucopyranosyl side chains, acts as a biotemplate for the preparation of asymmetric anisotropic gold and palladium nanoparticles with a distinct head-and-tail morphology, resembling nanosperms. This is caused by different glycosidic linkages in the structure of schizophyllan. While (1 → 6)-bound side chains are readily oxidized to dialdehydes, the two chain termini react asymmetrically. The reducing end is effectively silenced, whereas the non-reducing end is converted to reactive dialdehyde, resulting in an asymmetric distribution of reducing groups. Particle morphology is tunable by varying the degree of oxidation and the molecular weight, with best results obtained for schizophyllan with M w ~ 6.9 × 10 5 g mol −1 and a degree of oxidation of 30%, which yielded gold nanoparticles with a 33 ± 6 nm head and a 7 ± 1 nm thick tail and palladium nanoparticles with a 7 ± 1 nm head and 3 ± 1 nm thick tail. Both are highly active catalysts for the reduction of 4-nitrophenol (TOFs of 49 ± 5 min −1 and 115 ± 22 min −1 , respectively), and gold nanoparticles also exhibited SERS amplification.

title: Interaction and inhibition mechanism of molecular weight-regulated feruloylated oligosaccharides from rice bran with α-amylase
Polysaccharide esters in drug delivery: Translation from laboratory scale toward clinical use
abstract: Polysaccharide esters are bio-based, biocompatible, and biodegradable materials, displaying a broad chemical versatility and a potential for drug delivery applications. This review examines polysaccharides, bearing pendant ester functionalities, highlighting how the esterification strategies influence material properties, biological performances and translational potential. Representative synthetic strategies for esterifying carbohydrate scaffolds, including cyclodextrins, starch, cellulose, and related polysaccharides, are compared, with an emphasis on the relationship between chemical modification and resulting material properties. The literature shows that the degree, distribution, and chemical nature of ester substitution are key parameters governing aqueous solubility, drug loading, encapsulation, release behavior, and interactions with biological barriers. Strategically selected esterification can improve processability and enable the formation of soluble carriers, particulate systems, three-dimensional hydrogels, and surface brushes. However, extensive hydrophobic substitution may reduce water solubility, while poorly controlled substitution patterns and incomplete structural characterization limit reproducibility and meaningful comparison between studies. Reported in vivo studies, clinical investigations, and marketed formulations are highlighted, along with current challenges related to synthesis, characterization, and translation. Overall, polysaccharide esters offer a versatile, bio-based platform for tailoring drug delivery systems through chemical design, providing complementary advantages to conventional polyesters. However, further progress in synthetic control, analytical standardization, and translational validation will be essential for clinical advancement.

Scalable production of tailored cellulose esters via continuous reactive extrusion: Tuning degree of substitution and performance via reagent sequence
abstract: Mixed cellulose esters with short- and long-chain acyl groups were synthesized via continuous reactive extrusion in a recyclable 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium acetate (EmimOAc)/DMSO system, enabling one-step transesterification with precise control of the total degree of substitution (DS ≈ 2). Complete in situ dissolution of 10 wt% cellulose occurred in 150 s, and the subsequent esterification achieved near-quantitative (98–100%) conversion. Quantitative 13 C NMR revealed that the sequence of reagent addition effectively influences the substituent distribution along the cellulose backbone. Initiating the reaction with the short-chain acetylating agent partially attenuated the intrinsic reactivity hierarchy: acetyl groups favored both positions 6 and 3 (6 ≈ 3 > 2), while subsequent decanoyl groups favored position 6. In contrast, adding the bulky decanoylating agent first resulted in a more uniform substitution of decanoyl groups across positions 2, 3, and 6. Simultaneous feeding of both reagents preserved the preference for position 6. These distinct feeding strategies were associated with difference in material performance: the sequential acetylation-first method yielded films with up to 23% higher tensile strength, while the simultaneous feeding approach increased thermal stability by 68 °C. This approach enables scalable synthesis of mixed cellulose esters with tunable, predictable structure–property relationships.

title: Toward improved recycling of textiles: A study into selective de-crosslinking of cellulosic materials
abstract: Chemical crosslinking of cellulose-based textiles is employed to improve their fibrillation behavior and durability. However, the resulting covalent networks can restrict swelling, dissolution, and disintegration, thereby limiting recycling at end-of-life. In this study, the reversibility of crosslinking with dimethyloldihydroxyethyleneurea (DMDHEU) and 1,3,5-triacryloylhexahydro-1,3,5-triazine (TAHT) was investigated. To identify crosslinker-specific cleavage conditions, screenings with model compounds were conducted. The DMDHEU-linkages were cleaved under acidic conditions, whereas TAHT-linkers were removed by alkaline treatments. The identified conditions were transferred to the cellulose-based materials. Crosslinked cellulose exhibited impaired dissolution, and most modified samples were not amenable to representative solution-state characterization before crosslinker cleavage. The material before and after trigger-selective cleavage was characterized by elemental analysis, FTIR spectroscopy, solid-state NMR, dissolution studies, solution-state NMR, and gel-permeation chromatography. For commercial TAHT-crosslinked lyocell fibers, alkaline cleavage reduced the nitrogen content by 83% relative to the material prior to cleavage, with the remaining nitrogen content approaching the level of the untreated reference fibers. Acidic cleavage of the linkers in DMDHEU-modified cellulose resulted in up to 95% reduction of the incorporated nitrogen content. In all cases, the dissolution behavior was substantially improved, and the cellulose structure remained preserved. The results highlight the importance of end-of-life de-crosslinking approaches for cellulosic textiles.

Adhesive hydrogels reinforced with cellulose nanocrystal–amyloid-like protein composites
abstract: Adhesive hydrogels are widely used in soft tissue repair, but their performance depends on both bulk mechanical strength and interfacial adhesion during deformation. Here, cellulose nanocrystal–amyloid-like protein (CNC–ALP) composites were incorporated into an acrylamide/[2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl]trimethylammonium chloride network by UV copolymerization. Among the formulations prepared from dispersions with 1 wt% CNC and 0–30 wt% ALP, the C1A20-gel, prepared from the C1A20 dispersion, combined a Young's modulus of 38 kPa, a tensile strength of 249.6 kPa, and an elongation at break of approximately 912%. The composites provide functional groups that may contribute to multivalent interfacial interactions while reinforcing the polymer network. In a repeated adhesion–detachment test on glass, adhesion strength decreased from 115.5 kPa to 72 kPa over 20 cycles. On fresh porcine skin, C1A20-gel exhibited a mean lap-shear strength of 9.83 kPa and a peel-derived interfacial toughness of 103.82 J/m 2 . The preformed hydrogel maintained conformal contact with ex vivo tissues during manual deformation, and its extracts showed good cytocompatibility in the cell assays used here. These results support CNC–ALP composites as fillers for mechanically reinforced adhesive hydrogels.

title: Nanocellulose-based 3D printing inks: From material design to biomedical applications
Cyclodextrin polymers efficiently incorporate linezolid through multiple binding modes: insights from experiments and molecular simulations
abstract: Epichlorohydrin-crosslinked β-cyclodextrin polymers (pCDs) are versatile drug carriers that solubilize poorly water-soluble molecules and exhibit intrinsic biological activity. However, the broad dispersity and ill-defined architecture of conventionally synthesized pCDs have hindered structure–property correlations at the molecular level. Here, we report the synthesis of pCDs with well-defined molecular weights and low dispersities, fully characterized for composition, size, and supramolecular organization. All pCD fractions enabled substantially higher linezolid (LZD) solubilization than native βCD, with association constants independent of molecular weight. NMR spectroscopy revealed a tilted aromatic insertion geometry for LZD within the βCD cavity and identified additional drug interactions in inter-cavity microdomains unique to the polymer. An atomistic pCD model, constructed for the first time, was subjected to molecular docking and microsecond molecular dynamics simulations. LZD preferentially associated with inter-cavity regions rather than undergoing spontaneous cavity inclusion, with binding limited primarily by kinetic and steric constraints rather than geometric incompatibility. These findings establish that pCDs bind drugs through multiple complementary modes, and demonstrate experimentally grounded atomistic simulation as a powerful framework for rational design of carbohydrate-based drug delivery platforms.

Wheatinan – The exopolysaccharide from the non-phytopathogenic Erwinia sp. STN24
abstract: Erwinia are ubiquitous endophytes that colonize economically important crops. While some are phytopathogens, others exhibit beneficial plant growth-promoting traits. This is the case of the novel non-pathogenic Erwinia sp. STN24 strain, isolated from wheat. The production of exopolysaccharides (EPS) is one of the main virulence characteristics of pathogenic Erwinia species. In this work, it is hypothesized that this non-pathogenicity may be related with a different EPS structure. Sugar composition, methylation analysis, and NMR spectroscopy revealed a backbone of →3)-β- d -Gal p- (1 → 3)-α- d -Gal p- (1 → 6)-β- d -Gal p- (1→, with the α- d -Gal p decorated at O -6 with terminal β- d -Glc p and at O -4 with β- d -Glc p- (1 → 2)-α- d -Gal p- (1 → 4)-β- d -GlcA p- (1→. NMR also revealed acetylation, mainly at O -3 of →2)-α- d -Gal p- (1 → unit. This structure was named wheatinan, distinguished from pathogenic amylovoran by the lack of pyruvilated α- d -Gal p and the presence of β- d -Glc p- (1 → 2)-[3Ac]-α- d -Gal p- (1→. Wheatinan, Erwinia sp. STN24, or a combination of both, significantly enhanced the growth of Meski pepper seedlings, including increased stem and root lengths, leaf number and area, fresh weight, chlorophyll, and auxin contents, compared to control plants, without observation of disease symptoms. Overall, these findings highlight Erwinia sp. STN24 as a promising plant growth-promoting bacterium and its novel EPS wheatinan as a bioactive polysaccharide with potential applications in sustainable agriculture.

title: Decoding the glycan architecture of Fusobacterium gonidiaformans rough-type lipopolysaccharide: implications for lectin recognition and immune response
abstract: Fusobacterium gonidiaformans is a poorly characterized Gram-negative species of human urogenital and intestinal tracts, increasingly reported in puerperal infections, bacteremia, and inflammation-associated diseases. Although other Fusobacterium species have been extensively linked to pathogenic processes, the molecular determinants underlying host interaction of F. gonidiaformans remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the structural and immunological properties of its rough-type lipopolysaccharide (R-LPS), a major outer membrane glycoconjugate involved in innate immune recognition. Structural analyses combining compositional studies, NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry revealed a complex R-LPS characterized by a predominantly hexaacylated lipid A and a highly phosphorylated, heptose-rich core oligosaccharide displaying marked structural heterogeneity. Scattering analyses further demonstrated the formation of supramolecular assemblies in aqueous solution. Functional analyses showed that F. gonidiaformans R-LPS is recognized by a broad repertoire of innate immune lectins and selectively activates TLR4-dependent signaling, promotes dendritic cell maturation and moderates myeloid cell activation while eliciting only limited epithelial responses and attenuated pro-inflammatory activity compared with pro-inflammatory Escherichia coli LPS. These findings expand current knowledge of LPS diversity within the genus Fusobacterium and, more broadly, provide new insights into how structural variation within bacterial surface glycans shapes host recognition and innate immune responses.

Spatiotemporal reprogramming of hyaluronic acid hydrogel viscoelasticity through light-triggered dynamic covalent bond exchange
abstract: The ability to spatiotemporally program mechanical properties in soft materials is essential for emerging applications in adaptive materials, 3D cell cultures, and functional polymer systems. In particular, controlling viscoelasticity independent of network structure and crosslink density remains a fundamental challenge, as these properties are typically intrinsically coupled. Here, we introduce a light-responsive dynamic covalent hydrogel (DCH) platform that enables spatiotemporal control over mechanical properties by modulating network dynamics rather than network architecture. To achieve this, we designed light-responsive hyaluronic acid (HA) based DCHs crosslinked with dynamic hydrazone bonds and functionalized with coumarin-based photocages bearing latent hydroxylamine groups. Photolytic cleavage of these cages allowed on-demand release of hydroxylamines, which, upon uncaging, underwent dynamic exchange with the hydrazones. This light-mediated hydrazone-to-oxime conversion resulted in spatiotemporal modulation of hydrogel viscoelasticity. Photopatterning enabled mechanically heterogeneous microenvironments, as confirmed by nanoindentation mapping. Furthermore, bulk mechanical properties correlated with both photocage content and irradiation dose, providing a predictable framework for material design. This strategy enables mechanical reprogramming without changing crosslink density, providing an orthogonal route to tune hydrogel mechanics. By enabling user-defined and localized control over viscoelasticity, this platform establishes a versatile strategy for engineering cell-instructive matrices, adaptive soft devices, and next-generation programmable hydrogels.

Pickering-emulsion-mediated nanoscale interfacial engineering enables efficient long-chain hydrophobization of cellulose nanocrystals
abstract: Esterification-based hydrophobization of cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) suffers from a longstanding efficiency–sustainability tradeoff. Highly hydrophobic reactants exhibit low reactivity, whereas activation methods require toxic reagents, excess solvents, or energy-intensive processing. Herein we report a Pickering-emulsion-mediated nanoscale interfacial esterification strategy that addresses this challenge. CNCs function as both emulsion stabilizers and substrates, confining fatty acid droplets into hydrophobic domains that promote esterification of surface hydroxy groups by expelling the water byproduct from the oil droplets into the surrounding aqueous phase. The strategy is applicable to fatty acids with varying chain lengths with the surface degree of substitution increasing from 0.755 (C4) to 1.659 (C18), reversing the trend typically observed in conventional esterification. C18- g -CNCs show a water contact angle of 117.2°, stable dispersibility in nonpolar solvents, and a fivefold increase in film toughness (4.91 MJ m −3 ), while retaining high crystallinity (~76%) and soil biodegradability (>78% within 70 d). Technoeconomic and life-cycle assessments demonstrate reductions in production cost (51.2%) and global warming potential (80.4%) compared with acid-activated esterification, and successful reaction scaleup supports the process feasibility. Beyond CNCs, this work demonstrates the potential of Pickering-emulsion-mediated interfacial nanoreactors as a platform for efficient and sustainable surface engineering of biobased nanomaterials.
